newsitem.title: USA: American voters more upbeat this time around.
newsitem.headline: American voters more upbeat this time around.

text.p: They are bored, disinterested, cynical, but their anger is below the surface this time. Many of them won't even bother to vote while those that do will not be very passionate about their choice.
As the campaign enters its last few days, those are the descriptions that pollsters and voters are using to describe the mood of the American electorate.

The experts may disagree on exactly where to put the emphasis, but they agree that the 1996 presidential race has not engaged voters with the passion of four years ago when Bill Clinton, George Bush and Ross Perot argued over the soul of the country as a recession spurred economic fears.

With the economy appearing strong and no pressing foreign crises around, 1992 seems a long time ago and that appears to be benefitting the incumbent Clinton, who two years into his presidency was declared a dead duck by friend and foe alike.

Most polls have him with a double-digit lead ranging from 10 to 18 points although a poll conducted for Reuters by the John Zogby Group International showed on Saturday the race tightening with Clinton's lead dropping to only 3.8 points.
The pollsters say many voters are finding the 1996 race boring -- dominated by two men they have gotten used to, men who don't really disagree on much. And many voters yearn for a fresh face.
Republican Sen. Alfonse D'Amato of New York was quoted as telling a Harvard University audience that even Dole found the election boring and that explained why his campaign seems so lackluster.
Casual conversations with voters show no great enthusiasm and a grudging respect for Perot but only for raising the issues that Dole and Clinton seem to be ignoring.

Dentist John Zawadzinski of Clifton, New Jersey, says his phone has been jumping off the hook this year with calls from parties and candidates but he still can't make up his mind because basically Dole and Clinton leave him cold.

"I am undecided. I am not voting for Clinton because I don't trust the man. But I don't like Dole either," he said, adding that the only one he agrees with is his local bishop, who wrote an editorial complaining that politicians were disillusioning voters with their negative campaigning.
CBS polls say a lot of the anger that accompanied the 1992 and 1994 elections has dissipated because fewer people in 1996 fear losing their jobs.
"The mood is quiet. A lot of the anger has disappeared. We asked how many people feared losing their jobs and 85 percent said they didn't fit that category," said Anna Maria Arumi, a CBS pollster.

"We also found that 40 percent of Americans think the country is on the right track and while that might not seem like a big figure, you have to remember that in 1992 only 19 percent of Americans thought that," she added.
Andrew Kohut of the Pew Research Centre says indications are that turnout in Tuesday's election will be lower than 1992 -- probably just over 50 percent of eligible voters.
"They are turned off by the race between Clinton and Dole because they don't see it as a race. They don't think very much of Dole," he said.
Ninety million Americans eligible to vote in the elections may stay home from the polls, a survey by the Committee for the Study of the American Electorate said on Friday.
Jeff Alderman, the director of polling for ABC, says the big issues in the races are money and Medicare -- and Clinton has the edge on both issues.

"Money makes you happy and the economy is good. The voters are not angry. Many even think the country is headed in the right direction. While it is true that some voters have questions about Clinton's honesty, half the electorate thinks he has the moral stuff to be president," Alderman said.
He added, 'Given the choice between having an honest man or someone who cares about their problems, they opt for caring."
